item.title: Are Gay Men Really That Shallow?
item.description:
Bias

Are Gay Men Really That Shallow?

Personal Perspective: Why stereotypes persist, and how we can start to see past them.

Posted June 26, 2026

Key points
  • A growing genre of online discourse portrays gay men as shallow, image-obsessed, and emotionally unavailable.
  • Research finds higher rates of body dissatisfaction among gay men, closely linked to minority stress.
  • Confirmation bias is when we notice what supports a belief we have while overlooking everything else.
Source: Or Hakim / Unsplash

You've probably heard that gay men are image-obsessed, promiscuous, and unable to sustain relationships.

Are we image-obsessed, or did this single story come first, repeated until we internalized it as how we see ourselves, and eventually how others see us, too?

I was recently interviewed by Pat Brothwell, a journalist who writes about identity and culture, for a Pride Month piece exploring this phenomenon in his journalism.

He'd come across an earlier article I wrote drawing on Chimamanda Adichie's talk “The Danger of a Single Story,” one of my favorite talks, where she describes the consequences of using one narrative to define a person or a group.

As she puts it, the problem with a stereotype isn't that it's untrue, but that it's incomplete. It takes one story and makes it the only story.

Pat told me he'd been watching a single story spread through a growing genre of online discourse, where people make sweeping claims about “the gay community” being shallow, image-obsessed, emotionally unavailable, or incapable of commitment.

So why are we, both inside and outside the community, drawn to these broad narratives, and are they true? What's more, why does it matter?

A few things are happening at once, I told Pat. Part of it is introjection, the process by which we unconsciously take in the thoughts, beliefs, and attitudes of the people and culture around us. Most gay men grew up introjecting messages about who gay men are, and those narratives become part of how we see ourselves and each other—the single story.

I grew up without marriage ever being an option. Same-sex marriage wasn't legal nationwide until 2015, and for most of my life, gay male relationships weren't modeled for me. I had no sense of what two men in a healthy, loving relationship looked like. It wasn't technically even "real" in my consciousness. Going from the closet and the fear of being gay to almost no understanding of gay relationships informs how many gay men relate to one another.

For gay men, introjection can manifest as internalized homophobia, which influences the second component, projection, where we take what we unconsciously fear about ourselves and place it onto an entire group.

Part of it is also confirmation bias, our tendency to notice what supports a belief we already have while overlooking everything else. Once someone believes gay men are shallow or image-obsessed, they'll register every example that fits the single story and skip past the ones that don't.

As a therapist who specializes in working with gay men, I hear a lot of clients talk about the very aspects of the gay community Pat described. For many, the community can be a retraumatization of the childhood experiences of exclusion they were hoping to leave behind. I want to validate their experience because there are certainly elements that are true. I also want to help them develop insight into their schemas, or patterns of thinking, and look for the exceptions that challenge the single story.

As much as there are gay men who are emotionally unavailable and image-obsessed, there are also gay men who aren’t.

When we rely on the single story of gay men, it’s easy to see them as shallow or image-obsessed. Research shows that gay men have higher rates of body dissatisfaction than heterosexual men, which is clinically relevant in my work.

When we explore what's underneath, though, it’s often related to minority stress—the chronic stress gay men experience as a result of ongoing stigma, discrimination, and exclusion, from society, family, and early environments where their identity was ignored or invalidated. So the single story becomes a conversation about minority stress, and less about vanity.

By understanding the connection between unhealthy body standards and minority stress, we can challenge one of the more pervasive single stories about gay men.

Gay men are bombarded with images about body standards, and it's important to acknowledge how inescapable these images are, everything from pornography to social media to marketing at gay bars, to the images the media uses when reporting on gay men. Most marketing directed toward and about gay men relies on a narrow, sexualized standard of bodies.

Take, for example, the viral article Wired published earlier this year. The illustrations depicted gay men as hypersexualized stereotypes, including two limp wrists reaching out to give a handshake coming out of the zipper of their pants. Just now, I searched "gay men" in Google images, and the vast majority were shirtless and muscular.

Challenging the single story means asking whether the narrative we've accepted is true. Gay men are not a monolith, and our relationships, desires, and values are as diverse as we are. Shared identity doesn't mean shared experience.

The work of separating who we are from what we've internalized is at the heart of my forthcoming book, Becoming Worthy, which helps gay men heal shame, love themselves, and become worthy of the life they want.

The moment we trade the single story for a more complete one, we start relating to people as they are, rather than who we assume them to be.

item.title: Living in a Delusional World
item.description:
Anxiety

Living in a Delusional World

Anxiety about a complex world can lead people to embrace simple answers.

Posted June 26, 2026

Key points
  • Rumors and myths may appeal to anxious people because they provide simple explanations for complex situations.
  • Delusional people typically don't have a mental illness, but have been duped into believing rumors or myths.
  • Moving people away from their delusional views of the world requires finding common goals and motivations.
  • New insights from trusted sources helps people loosen their grip on rumors and delusional views.
Delusional Thinking Can Reduce Anxiety
Source: Mindworld / Pixabay

I’ve written about why people embrace misinformation, rumors, and myths, i.e., why they accept things as true without evidence or substantive support from experts. Stephen Colbert saw the rise in this phenomenon in 2005, and coined the term “truthiness.”[i] This describes a quality of things that seem like they should be true, which people just believe due to a "gut feeling."

A related phenomenon is when people begin to believe something simply because they hear it many times. The psychology term for this is the “Illusory Truth Effect.”[ii] Marketers use this in ad campaigns by repeatedly hitting people with the same messages for their new products, e.g., “bigger, better, and faster.”

The common theme here is that people are willing to accept things that are not true if it makes sense to them – especially if it makes it easier for them to “identify” a cause or a bad actor to blame, rather than having to accept that something was their fault, was just an accident, or was an “act of God.” That delusional “reasoning” can reduce their anxiety about complex life situations.

How to Deal With Delusional People

“I didn’t do it!” was a stock reply from the cartoon character Bart Simpson in the early years of The Simpsons TV show. That typifies a 10-year-old’s view of the world, in which they think that lying can make people believe they are innocent of any misdeeds. However, as the show (and Bart) matured, he stopped saying it – particularly after an episode where he became famous for saying it, and was parodied and ridiculed.[iii]

However, if you’re dealing with a flesh-and-blood adult who is living in their own delusional bubble about some important issue (or issues) like climate change, politics, vaccines, infectious diseases, or whether or not birds are real[iv] – how you interact with them can be important, particularly if they are a family member or someone you work with.

As I outlined in my book Reversing Misinformation: How to Help Your Family, Friends & Community, when someone believes false rumors, myths, or incorrect statements about factual things, (i.e., misinformation), trying to correct them is almost always counterproductive – unless you enjoy having arguments about what are or are not facts. And unfortunately, such “my facts v. your facts” arguments are more challenging now because almost any statement can be backed up with “something” from the internet.

So rather than having those types of counter-productive arguments, what you – as someone they know, and hopefully view as a trusted source of information – should do with a person living in a delusional world (assuming they don’t have an actual, serious psychological illness like schizophrenia or bipolar disorder where their delusions and paranoia can make them dangerous and they are in need of professional medical help), is to get them to explain their world views to you. You want to do this so you can understand why they believe what they do, explore with them the basis for their mistrust of mainstream information sources and experts (who they may call “so-called experts”), and identify their motivations and goals, such as wanting themselves and their family and friends to be healthy, or for elections to be run fairly and honestly.

Your common goals and motivations are the basis for having productive conversations, and may provide you with the opportunity to get them to explore alternative ideas. This could lead them to develop some cognitive dissonance and question the accuracy of their views.

This process starts sort of like two people yelling at each other from the tops of two mountains: They can’t hear each other, and the result is just anger and frustration. But if the two people meet in the valley — where they share a common view of the landscape — they can have a constructive conversation.

To get on the same communications plane with a delusional person (who is not experiencing a clinical psychotic episode), you need to listen, understand their viewpoints of reality, and identify common grounds of goals and motivations. Finding a way to dance along a common path with them will be much more productive than trying to wrestle them off their train of thought and drag them to see your perspectives and reality from atop an unfamiliar mountain.

Delusional Thinking Can Reduce Anxiety
Source: Mindworld / Pixabay

Why People Use Delusions to Cope with Anxiety

Rational, thinking people may embrace rumors and myths, and grab onto delusions, because it can make the complexities of modern life – and particularly bad things happening to them – less upsetting, since blame can be placed upon others.

Constructively talking with such people in your life requires understanding their delusional viewpoints so you can identify common goals and motivations, such as wanting people to become and stay healthy. The next step is talking with them in a collaborative way to start introducing alternative possibilities that may lead them to develop cognitive dissonance and question their belief in the rumors and myths that led them to have an unreal perspective about important things in their lives, like health, vaccines, elections, or climate change.

item.title: When Anxiety Runs the Room
item.description:
Leadership

When Anxiety Runs the Room

What "Inside Out" taught me about leadership, joy, and emotions we don't let speak.

Posted June 26, 2026

Key points
  • Sadness, when allowed to speak, often carries the clearest signal in the room.
  • Anxiety-driven leadership can look like excellence, until it becomes the only frequency a leader operates on.
  • The best leaders hold the full emotional range and don't let any single emotion run the room.

On a recent flight, I did what I often do: I put on a children's movie.

I'm not subtle about it. I laugh out loud. I've been known to tear up. On this particular flight, I was watching Inside Out 2, and somewhere over the middle of the country, I was laughing hard enough that the man beside me finally looked over.

"Whatever you're watching," he said, "it must be good."

"It's Inside Out," I told him.

He smiled, genuinely glad to see someone laughing that hard, and went back to his iPad.

There wasn't time to explain. I wasn't laughing because the film was silly. I was laughing because I recognized everyone in it. Including myself.

Joy is my favorite, as you can see by the photo, and I cried when Imagination Land was destroyed.

In the first Inside Out, Joy is the one running Riley's emotional control panel. She's optimistic, fast-moving, fiercely protective, and utterly convinced that if she can just keep things positive enough, everything will be okay. She's not wrong to care. But she makes one costly mistake: she keeps Sadness out of the room.

Sadness carries the honest signals. The grief of losing something real. The acknowledgment that things aren't fine. Joy doesn't see her as useful. She sees her as a risk.

And here's what the film gets exactly right. When Joy runs everything, and Sadness gets locked out, Riley doesn't feel better. She goes numb. Everything looks okay from the outside, and nothing is actually working on the inside.

This applies to every organization, in some form, because we are human.

Leaders who keep things positive, relentlessly, reflexively, and sometimes manipulatively, create cultures where the real story never surfaces: the struggling team member who stays quiet because the climate isn't safe for struggle; the strategic risk nobody names because the leader has already decided how it will go; the early warning signs that get softened into silence because this team doesn't do negativity.

They're not bad leaders. They care deeply. That's usually the problem. They're so invested in the vision of being right and the team being okay that they've unconsciously made it hard to hear when it isn't.

Joy means well. That's exactly what makes her dangerous when she's running the room alone.

Inside Out 2 introduces a new character. If the first film was about Joy, the second one belongs to Anxiety.

She arrives on Riley's control panel like a small hurricane. She's got plans within plans, and contingencies for the contingencies. She is trying to protect Riley from every form of hurt: rejection, failure, humiliation, and being left out. She works harder than anyone. She never stops.

She also eventually locks Joy in a vault, silences Sadness, and runs the entire system on one frequency, "What if this goes wrong?"

I've sat across from this leader, too. They're often highly capable, which is why they've been given the most to carry. They over-prepare every meeting. They solve objections before anyone has raised them. They absorb more than their share and tell you they're fine.

They're running on anxiety and calling it excellence.

The tricky thing is that it works, for a while. Anxiety gets things done. She keeps disasters at bay. At certain moments in a career, she's exactly what the situation demands. The problem is when she becomes the permanent operating system. When every decision gets filtered through "what could go wrong," and there's no room left for curiosity, or joy, or the kind of honest sadness that tells you something actually needs to change, that's not excellence. It's not even sustainable.

What the film eventually shows, and what I see in my work, is that the answer isn't silencing any of these voices. It's creating enough space for more than one of them to be heard.

Anxiety has real information. Joy is not the enemy. Sadness, when she's allowed to speak, often carries the clearest signal in the room.

The leaders I most admire aren't the ones who have mastered positivity or conquered their anxiety. They're the ones who have learned to hold the full emotional range and let it inform them without letting any one voice run the show.

That's harder than it sounds. It requires a kind of inner permission that high-performing people often struggle with: the permission to feel something other than in control.

Source: Laura Berger

But when they get there, when the room can hold both hope and difficulty, both ambition and honest reckoning, something shifts. People tell them what's actually happening, and decisions get better. Trust deepens. The culture becomes something people want to be part of rather than something they learn to perform.

The man beside me never asked what about the movie made me both laugh and cry throughout the flight.

If he had, I would have told him, this is one of my favorite movies because the characters represent our full range of emotions.

It turns out that's not a bad description of what it looks like to lead well.

Sometimes the clearest mirrors find you at 36,000 feet, on a Tuesday, watching something you weren't supposed to take seriously.

item.title: Why Nostalgia Is Reshaping Pop Culture
item.description:
Nostalgia

Why Nostalgia Is Reshaping Pop Culture

Why looking back can feel more comforting than moving forward.

Posted June 26, 2026

Key points
  • Nostalgia helps regulate emotions and reconnect you to meaningful past experiences.
  • Familiar media feels comforting during times of stress and uncertainty.
  • Pop culture reflects our need for connection, continuity, and emotional grounding.
  • Using nostalgia intentionally can support growth instead of avoiding the present.
Source: nana / Pexels

If you’ve recently rewatched an older rom-com, found yourself singing along to an early 2000s song, or felt a strange sense of excitement seeing a familiar cast reunite on your screen, you’re not alone. Nostalgia is often used when describing a feeling of longing and sadness for the past.

From a psychological perspective (and according to the American Psychological Association), nostalgia is a bittersweet emotional experience normally triggered by our senses. While often associated with feelings of loneliness, it doesn't have to be that way.

Instead of thinking of nostalgia as looking back, it can be used to form a connection with a simpler, seemingly happier version of yourself, to reminisce with others about the past and bring that into the present, or to things you used to like but have not made time for.

When used intentionally, nostalgia can function as a way to regulate emotions, helping people return to a more grounded state when the present feels overwhelming.

Why familiarity feels easier right now

Sitting back and watching “The Devil Wears Prada” again in time for the sequel, or “How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days,” isn’t just you being lazy or nostalgic for no reason. People tend to rewatch or re-listen to pop culture from earlier in their lives because it feels familiar. You know what to expect, you already know how the story ends, even with all the twists and turns, and you can sing along without thinking. Knowing what will happen creates a sense of stability in a time that may feel unpredictable.

Between global conflicts, financial stress, and a general sense of uneasiness, the world right now feels uncertain. Seeing Hilary Duff release new music that sounds like it could have come out in 2012, or watching legacy acts return for residencies, can feel like a break from that stress. Even going to the movies to watch a new version of an old favorite carries that same effect.

These moments aren’t just about entertainment. They reconnect people to a period in their lives that felt more defined and easier to navigate.

What nostalgia actually does psychologically

Nostalgia is tied to how people process identity and emotional experiences. Research shows that nostalgic reflection can improve mood, increase feelings of connection, and help people make sense of where they are in their lives. These feelings can help during highly stressful moments or periods of transition in your life.

Looking back offers a reference point and a reminder that stability, happiness, or clarity have existed before, even if they feel distant. And more importantly, that they can exist again.

In that sense, nostalgia doesn’t pull people away from the present. If anything, it gives them something to work with inside it.

Why pop culture keeps returning to the past

Pop culture tends to reflect what people are already seeking. From fashion trends (since when are low-rise jeans making a comeback?) to how we consume media. And right now, that includes familiarity, emotional connection, and continuity.

Reboots, reunions, and sequels provide all three, allowing people to revisit something familiar without fully engaging with something new. It’s not about avoiding change or new things as much as it is about revisiting meaning and connection.

For instance, when Joshua Jackson and Katie Holmes appeared on the red carpet for their latest movie together, it brought fans back to Dawson’s Creek. Beyond bringing back just Pacey and Joey, it also brought audiences back to a time, a feeling, and a version of themselves that existed alongside it.

That connection is what keeps people engaged.

When nostalgia becomes something else

As with all things, anything in excess can be considered harmful. Relying on the past to avoid the present can limit how you engage with what’s happening now.

The goal isn’t to stay in those memories, but to understand why they feel important. There’s a difference between revisiting something meaningful and wishing to remain there.

Research has shown that excessive nostalgia can sometimes reinforce avoidance patterns, particularly when people use it to disengage from current stressors rather than process them. While this doesn’t make nostalgia harmful, it does highlight the importance of balance and the importance of analyzing why we’re revisiting the same things. Is it to help us cope, or is it becoming a crutch to escape our current reality?

How to use nostalgia without getting stuck in it

Nostalgia can be helpful when used with the intention of understanding the present a little better, rather than escaping it.

One way to approach this is by paying attention to what you’re drawn to. If you keep going back to a certain song, movie, or time in your life, it usually reflects something you need now. It could be comfort, connection, stability, or even a sense of identity that feels less clear in the present.

But instead of staying in that moment, try to identify what about it felt meaningful. Was it the relationships you had? The sense of possibility? The pace of life?

Once you recognize that, the goal becomes finding ways to bring pieces of that feeling into your current life and reconnecting with what made it feel significant. This self-reflection is what keeps nostalgia from turning into avoidance, allowing it to function as a tool rather than a place to stay and hide.

Bringing it back to the present

Nostalgia works best when it’s used as a reference, not a goal to achieve again. It can be easy to think of the past as simpler or easier, but that isn’t always accurate. There were moments of uncertainty then, too.

Looking back now, it becomes clearer that things worked out in ways you may not have expected. That perspective is part of what makes nostalgia useful.

The moments people look back on now were once ordinary. At some point, today will be viewed in the same way. Remembering that can shift how the present is experienced.

Instead of trying to return to what felt easier, the focus becomes recognizing what feels meaningful now, while still in it.

item.title: Columbine, Shared Trauma, and Being a Survivor-Teacher
item.description:
Mass Shootings

Columbine, Shared Trauma, and Being a Survivor-Teacher

Expecting teachers to act as protectors distracts from institutional solutions.

Posted June 26, 2026

Key points
  • Columbine survival leaves a lasting somatic toll, triggering chronic PTSD and nightmares.
  • Survivor-teachers battle a constant baseline of trauma, fear, and survivor's guilt.
  • Active-shooter drills and arming teachers cause severe stress and ruin classroom trust.
  • Global examples prove strict firearm laws remove ambient fear and prevent mass casualties.

School shootings are the devastating symptom of systemic collapses. Ultimately, a society is only as healthy as the violence it creates and fails to prevent.1

The Columbine massacre on April 20, 1999, remains the grim anchor point for the modern era of American school shootings. During my interview with Michelle Markert-Porter, she recalled that she was a senior with just one month left until graduation when the Columbine shooting occurred. Caught in the cafeteria when the gunfire began, she fled upstairs into a science classroom filled with terrified fourteen-year-old freshmen and a teacher. Together, they spent three hours barricaded inside, being forced to watch the news on a classroom television to decipher what was happening just beyond their locked door.

While they survived physically uninjured, the psychological sanctuary of the school environment was permanently shattered. The arrival of the SWAT team, rather than bringing immediate relief, introduced a jarring, highly traumatic confrontation with reality—a stark confirmation that their school had transformed into a war zone.

Decades later, the internal psychological landscape of a survivor does not simply heal; it adapts, often dragging the past into the present through chronic trauma responses. Now a teacher and researcher living in New Zealand, Michelle notes that the somatic memory of Columbine remains deeply embedded. While living in Texas, Michelle recalls that loud noises like a car backfiring could trigger acute post-traumatic stress disorder, insomnia, and nightmares.

This prolonged state of psychological dysregulation is a common thread among those who lived through school shootings. In her doctoral research, which included interviews with eleven Columbine survivors who also chose to enter the teaching profession, Michelle found a pervasive baseline of trauma. Her participants reported chronic hypervigilance—such as arriving at public spaces thirty minutes early to scan for exits or keeping sharp scissors hidden in their desks—alongside deeper systemic struggles like addiction, eating disorders, survivor’s guilt, and the conscious decision by some to never bring children into what they perceive as an inherently dangerous world.

Michelle states, “Resilience doesn’t mean we’re just fine, or that everything’s back to normal. The cost isn’t talked about enough, and the growth is never worth the trauma.”

The Toxic Expectation of Clinical Containment

One of the most insidious developments in modern education is the unspoken expectation that teachers must function as final defensive shields. Michelle’s research exposes a resentment within the teaching community regarding this forced role. Michelle states that educators feel that they are increasingly expected to be hyperaware of psychological red flags, act as frontline behavioral investigators, and ultimately lay down their lives for their students. This structural burden is heavily compounded by the implementation of hyperrealistic active-shooter simulations and lockdown drills. While standard lockdown protocols can be useful for minor crises, Michelle emphasizes that live simulations are damaging and unsupported by data.

Even in New Zealand, where gun violence is rare due to common gun law restrictions, conducting these drills remains a source of immense stress, occasionally causing her to dissociate while students—steeped in a detached, media-driven perception of violence—treat the protocol as a game or act out shooter fantasies.

Forcing teachers to act as both frontline police and mental health clinicians traps them under a difficult burden of care. It forces an educator to simultaneously secure a physical perimeter and contain an escalating mental health crisis marked by homicidal and suicidal ideation—a grueling combination of tactical defense and psychiatric intervention. The burden is made heavier by the persistent political push to arm teachers, a concept that Michelle and her research participants universally reject. Forcing an educator to carry lethal force is not a clinical or logical solution. It is an ideological evasion that demands a teacher prepare to potentially kill someone else’s child, fundamentally destroying the relational trust required to cultivate a healthy holding environment in the classroom.

A Geography of Safety: The Global Contrast

The stark ideological contrast between the United States and the rest of the world becomes clear when observing how different societies manage systemic risk. Having spent four years teaching within the New Zealand education system, Michelle describes an ecosystem characterized by structural openness and a relative absence of ambient fear. In Wellington, school buildings remain physically open, windows are kept unbarred, and students routinely interact with their natural surroundings without the constant psychological threat of an active shooter.

The fundamental difference lies in a simpler reality: the absence of widespread firearm access. While New Zealand contends with its own domestic challenges, including high rates of bullying and a strained mental health infrastructure, these issues do not escalate into catastrophic mass casualty events because the physical means of mass destruction are strictly regulated.

Ultimately, the trajectory of the survivor-teacher reveals that mass violence is a preventable choice rather than an inevitable social reality. While American public discourse around school shootings frequently focuses on complex factors like mental health and media consumption, less emphasis is often placed on exploring the direct impact of firearm availability. Seeing a society operate successfully under a completely different paradigm allowed Michelle to find a sense of clinical hope, confirming that alternative structural models can protect both children and their educators.

We must look with deeper compassion at the impossible weight we have placed on teachers’ shoulders. True school safety relies heavily on fostering deep human connections and enacting thoughtful legislative reforms. Moving beyond a focus on tactical fortifications helps lessen the immense responsibility currently placed on educators to manage a broader societal crisis.
